main.title: Armored Core 2
main.subtitle: A mercenary career moves to Mars
main.summary: Armored Core 2 is FromSoftware's PlayStation 2 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 3 August 2000. Decades after the earlier trilogy, the colonisation of Mars has created another setting for corporate conflict and paid military work. The player assembles an Armored Core, takes contracts and confronts the Frighteners, a force threatening the established order. The move to new hardware gives the machines another level of detail, but the central relationship remains familiar. A battle tests decisions made in the garage, and its rewards make the next set of modifications possible.

cards.heading: A mercenary career moves to Mars
cards.text: Armored Core 2 is FromSoftware's PlayStation 2 mecha combat game, first released in Japan on 3 August 2000. Decades after the earlier trilogy, the colonisation of Mars has created another setting for corporate conflict and paid military work. The player assembles an Armored Core, takes contracts and confronts the Frighteners, a force threatening the established order. The move to new hardware gives the machines another level of detail, but the central relationship remains familiar. A battle tests decisions made in the garage, and its rewards make the next set of modifications possible.

cards.heading: Prepare one machine for several kinds of work
cards.text: Missions and Arena duels give a customised machine different tasks. A build that carries enough firepower for one contract may need another balance of speed or endurance against a rival pilot. The player learns how parts work together rather than treating each upgrade as an isolated improvement. Local multiplayer adds another test, allowing two players to confront one another with their own designs. The garage therefore supplies a continuing problem to solve: what should be changed after the last encounter, and which useful capability might be lost in making that adjustment?

cards.heading: An early PlayStation 2 showcase for the series
cards.text: Mechanical artist Shōji Kawamori returned, while a group including Tsukasa Saitoh and Kota Hoshino supplied the music. Armored Core 2 accompanied the PlayStation 2's North American launch in October 2000, with Europe following in January 2001. Another Age expanded this period of the series the following year. The game carries the original trilogy's workshop and mercenary structure onto a new machine without removing the need for deliberate preparation. Its attraction comes from seeing a personal design leave the garage and discovering whether the idea behind it survives contact with the battlefield.

main.title: Grandia II
main.summary: Grandia II is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts originally for the Dreamcast console as part of their Grandia series.

cards.text: Grandia II is a role-playing video game developed by Game Arts originally for the Dreamcast console as part of their Grandia series. Initially released in Japan by Game Arts in August 2000, the game was published by Ubi Soft in North America in December 2000 and in Europe in February 2001. Grandia II was later ported to PlayStation 2, where it was released worldwide throughout 2002, and for Windows exclusively in North America and Europe later that year.

An enhanced port, based on the Dreamcast version and titled Grandia II Anniversary Edition, was released by GungHo Online Entertainment for Steam and GOG.com in August 2015. A high-definition remaster of the game and the original Grandia was released for Nintendo Switch in August 2019; an associated update for the Anniversary Edition was released in October 2019. The PlayStation 4 and Xbox One versions were released in March 2024.

The game was developed by many of the same staff members who worked on the original Grandia, including music composer Noriyuki Iwadare. However, it was designed around creating a more "mature" product than the previous title and the first in the series to feature fully three-dimensional graphics.

The game is set in a fantasy world thousands of years after a battle between Granas, the god of light, and Valmar, the god of darkness, nearly destroyed the planet until Valmar was split into pieces and scattered across the land. In the aftermath of the battle, the Church of Granas has led humanity to prosperity by spreading the word of good. However, when a young mercenary named Ryudo is charged to protect a songstress from the church named Elena, their journey reveals that the church's history, as well as the history of the world, is not all it seems.

While the original Dreamcast version of the game received a largely positive response from critics in Japan and the West, its later ports to the PlayStation 2 and PC were typically seen as inferior due to a combination of technical shortcomings and other high-profile games released during the transition.

main.title: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins
main.subtitle: Meet the assassins before their first mission
main.summary: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins is Acquire's PlayStation stealth game, first released in North America on 8 August 2000. A prequel to Tenchu, it follows the younger Rikimaru and Ayame alongside their fellow ninja Tatsumaru as the Burning Dawn threatens their world. Missions again reward approaching an enemy without being discovered, using observation and tools to make a dangerous place manageable. The earlier point in the characters' lives gives familiar abilities another context. The player sees how these assassins became the figures introduced in the first game.

cards.heading: Meet the assassins before their first mission
cards.text: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins is Acquire's PlayStation stealth game, first released in North America on 8 August 2000. A prequel to Tenchu, it follows the younger Rikimaru and Ayame alongside their fellow ninja Tatsumaru as the Burning Dawn threatens their world. Missions again reward approaching an enemy without being discovered, using observation and tools to make a dangerous place manageable. The earlier point in the characters' lives gives familiar abilities another context. The player sees how these assassins became the figures introduced in the first game.

cards.heading: Leave fewer reasons for the alarm
cards.text: Missions take the ninja through varied locations, from farmland and bamboo forests to ships and caverns. The player studies guards, chooses an approach and uses equipment to avoid or quietly remove an obstacle. Performance is ranked after completion, including how often the character was spotted. Better ranks unlock additional gadgets, connecting careful play to new options in later attempts. Returning to a mission can therefore mean improving the route rather than simply finishing it again. A successful run is one in which the plan leaves little opportunity for the enemy to respond.

cards.heading: Build a place for another ninja
cards.text: The Mission Editor allows layouts, characters and objectives to be arranged into a custom assignment. It gives the player a chance to think about stealth from the other side: where a guard should stand, what a route should demand and how an objective should be reached. Noriyuki Asakura returned to compose the music. Activision requested the sequel after the first game's success, and reviewers generally welcomed its refinements. The editor adds a particularly clear extension of Tenchu's design, turning the player from someone reading a guarded space into someone constructing one.

main.title: Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble
main.subtitle: Nintendo · Game Boy Color
main.summary: Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble is Nintendo's Game Boy Color action-puzzle game about rolling Kirby through stages by tilting the handheld itself. Sensors inside its distinctive pink cartridge read the movement and translate it into the character's direction. Dream Land has lost its stars, giving Kirby a reason to pursue King Dedede through the obstacle courses. The player looks down on a ball-like hero whose movement depends on the angle of the screen being held, joining the physical object and the world displayed inside it in one unusually direct action.

cards.heading: Move the whole Game Boy to guide Kirby
cards.text: Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble is Nintendo's Game Boy Color action-puzzle game about rolling Kirby through stages by tilting the handheld itself. Sensors inside its distinctive pink cartridge read the movement and translate it into the character's direction. Dream Land has lost its stars, giving Kirby a reason to pursue King Dedede through the obstacle courses. The player looks down on a ball-like hero whose movement depends on the angle of the screen being held, joining the physical object and the world displayed inside it in one unusually direct action.

cards.heading: A small flick becomes a jump
cards.text: Tilting controls the roll, while a quick movement of the machine can pop Kirby into the air. The player balances momentum, direction and the timing needed to cross hazards before the stage's timer expires. Clock tiles and collected clocks provide extra time, making the route a choice between the destination and useful detours. The controls ask for awareness of the hands as well as the screen. A movement intended to correct the next turn also changes the angle from which the player is watching it happen.

cards.heading: A familiar character makes a sensor understandable
cards.text: Red stars hidden through the stages open more demanding versions of the worlds, encouraging a return once the unusual controls become comfortable. Nintendo released the cartridge in Japan in 2000 and North America in 2001. Kirby's round shape makes the hardware's purpose easy to understand: an apparently soft ball rolls in the direction the player tips the machine. The design turns an unfamiliar input into a recognisable toy-like action, then develops a complete obstacle course around learning to perform that action accurately.

main.title: ISS Pro Evolution 2
main.subtitle: A larger league before the name changed
main.summary: ISS Pro Evolution 2 is Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo's PlayStation football game, first released in Japan on 24 August 2000. It extends the previous game's on-field play and Master League, arriving in Europe in March 2001. The club competition now contains two divisions and twenty-four teams, giving promotion and the development of a squad a broader structure. It became the final entry in this branch to carry the ISS name before Pro Evolution Soccer. The familiar combination of immediate matches and a longer club project was already taking a recognisable form.

cards.heading: A larger league before the name changed
cards.text: ISS Pro Evolution 2 is Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo's PlayStation football game, first released in Japan on 24 August 2000. It extends the previous game's on-field play and Master League, arriving in Europe in March 2001. The club competition now contains two divisions and twenty-four teams, giving promotion and the development of a squad a broader structure. It became the final entry in this branch to carry the ISS name before Pro Evolution Soccer. The familiar combination of immediate matches and a longer club project was already taking a recognisable form.

cards.heading: Build towards a better place in the league
cards.text: More clubs and the additional division give the Master League a longer path, making the team's results part of a competition that continues beyond one fixture. The player still has to create opportunities on the field through movement, passing and the timing of an attack. The sequel refines those interactions, giving an experienced player reasons to adjust the pace of familiar moves. Partial licensing introduces some real player names, while other presentation remains approximate. The central attraction is the football itself and the steady improvement of the group being taken into the next match.

cards.heading: Different editions around the same football game
cards.text: The Japanese release included under-twenty-three national teams connected to the Sydney Olympic competition, material absent from the European edition. North America did not receive this release, following the earlier ESPN MLS GameNight variation instead. ISS Pro Evolution 2 won the sports-game award at the 2001 BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Awards. Its position at the end of the ISS Pro naming period makes it a bridge between the PlayStation series and the more widely recognised Pro Evolution Soccer identity, carrying forward a league mode and style of football that had already earned a dedicated audience.

main.title: Dragon Quest VII
main.summary: Dragon Quest VII: Fragments of the Forgotten Past, known in Japan as Dragon Quest VII: Warriors of Eden, is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Heartbeat and ArtePiazza, and published by Enix for the PlayStation.

cards.text: Dragon Quest VII: Fragments of the Forgotten Past, known in Japan as Dragon Quest VII: Warriors of Eden, is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by Heartbeat and ArtePiazza, and published by Enix for the PlayStation. The game was produced by Yuji Horii, who has presided over the Dragon Quest series since its inception. Artwork and character designs were once again provided by Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama, the artist responsible for all previous Dragon Quest games. It was released in North America in 2001 under the title Dragon Warrior VII. The game received a remake on the Nintendo 3DS in Japan in 2013; the remake was released in English under the title Dragon Quest VII: Fragments of the Forgotten Past in 2016. A version of the game for Android and iOS was released in Japan in 2015. Another remake, entitled Dragon Quest VII Reimagined, was released for Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, and PC on February 5, 2026.

The game follows the Hero and his friends as they discover secrets about the mysterious islands surrounding their home of Estard. Through some ancient ruins, they are transported to the pasts of various islands and must defeat evil in each new location. Game mechanics are largely unchanged from previous games in the series, although an extensive Class system allows players to customize their characters.

Dragon Quest VII: Fragments of the Forgotten Past is the seventh installment of the popular Dragon Quest series of role playing games, and is the successor to 1995's Dragon Quest VI for the Super Famicom. An immediate success upon release, Dragon Warrior VII's sales totalled 4.06 million by April 6, 2001, making it the best-selling PlayStation game in Japan, and is an Ultimate Hits title. It was the first main series Dragon Quest title to be released outside Japan since the release of Dragon Quest IV in North America in 1992, the last Dragon Quest title to be released in North America with the Dragon Warrior name, and the last Dragon Quest game outside of Japan to be published by Enix, before merging with Squaresoft in 2003 to form Square Enix.

main.title: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2
main.summary: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 is a 2000 skateboarding video game developed by Neversoft for PlayStation and Natsume for Game Boy Color.

cards.text: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 is a 2000 skateboarding video game developed by Neversoft for PlayStation and Natsume for Game Boy Color. Published by Activision, it is the second installment in the Tony Hawk's series of sports games, and was released for the PlayStation in 2000, with subsequent ports to Windows and Dreamcast alongside a distinct version for Game Boy Color the same year. In 2001, the game was ported to Mac OS, Mac OS X, Nintendo 64, and Xbox (as part of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x), alongside a separate version for Game Boy Advance by Vicarious Visions. The game was later ported to Windows Mobile and Windows Phone devices in 2006 and to iPhone OS devices in 2010.

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 uses the same game engine as its predecessor while improving the graphics and gameplay, most notably with the introduction of manuals and cash rewards. The game takes place in a three-dimensional urban environment permeated by an ambience of punk rock and hip-hop music. The player takes control of a variety of skateboarders and either performs skateboarding tricks or collects certain objects. The game offers several modes of gameplay, including a career mode in which the player must complete objectives and evolve their character's attributes with earned profits, a free-play mode in which the player may skate without any given objective, a multiplayer mode that features a number of competitive games, and a level editor that allows the player to create customized levels.

Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 was critically acclaimed upon release and is considered one of the greatest video games ever created, as well as the highest-rated sports video game. All versions of the game were praised, with critics lauding its addictive gameplay, large environments, detailed graphics, fluid and precise controls, customization features and soundtrack, with some minor criticisms directed at the lack of a first-person camera and the truncated soundtrack of the Nintendo 64 version. A sequel, Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3, was released in 2001.

main.title: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn
main.summary: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment for Windows in September 2000.

cards.heading: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn
cards.text: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn is a 2000 role-playing video game developed by BioWare and published by Interplay Entertainment for Windows in September 2000. It is the sequel to 1998's Baldur's Gate. Following its predecessor, the game takes place in the Forgotten Realms, a fantasy campaign setting, and is based on the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd edition rules. Powered by BioWare's Infinity Engine, Baldur's Gate II uses an isometric perspective and pausable real-time gameplay. The player controls a party of up to six characters, one of whom is the player-created protagonist; the others are certain characters recruited from the game world.

cards.heading: Irenicus and the city of Athkatla
cards.text: Much of Baldur's Gate II takes place in and around Athkatla, a city in the country of Amn. Opening shortly after the events of Baldur's Gate, the game continues the story of the protagonist, Gorion's Ward, whose unique heritage has now drawn the attention of Jon Irenicus, a powerful and sinister mage. The storyline revolves around the machinations of Irenicus and the player's encounters with him.

cards.heading: BioWare builds on player feedback
cards.text: Development began in January 1999. BioWare set out to improve upon the first Baldur's Gate in every way possible. From a list of constructive criticism—compiled from the suggestions of fans, reviews, and internal suggestions—a list of features to be added to the game was distilled: some of these were 800×600 resolution, 3D support, and character kits. For Baldur's Gate, the game's engine and content were being developed at the same time, whereas with Baldur's Gate II, the engine was working from the start. Having a completed engine meant they could direct their efforts towards making content, instead of focusing on basic functionality.

cards.heading: Acclaim and the conclusion of the saga
cards.text: Shadows of Amn received critical acclaim, being praised for its gameplay, artwork, and voice acting, and is widely regarded as one of the best video games ever made. GameSpy, GameSpot, and IGN awarded it their "Role-Playing Game of the Year" awards for 2000, and the game has sold more than two million units. An expansion pack, Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal, was released in 2001. This well-received expansion, besides adding a large dungeon and enhancements to the game, concluded the main storyline. Shadows of Amn and Throne of Bhaal have been included together in various compilations. In 2013, an enhanced version of Baldur's Gate II was released, carrying the title Baldur's Gate II: Enhanced Edition and using an updated version of the Infinity Engine. A sequel, Baldur's Gate 3, developed by Larian Studios, was released in 2023.

main.title: Skies of Arcadia
main.subtitle: Air pirates on an open horizon
main.summary: On November 14, 2000, Sega of America brings Skies of Arcadia to Dreamcast in North America.

cards.heading: Air pirates on an open horizon
cards.text: Overworks' Skies of Arcadia reached Dreamcast in North America on November 14, 2000. Produced by Rieko Kodama, the RPG follows air pirate Vyse through a world of floating islands. Searching for unknown places, fighting with a party and commanding a ship share the journey. Its bright skies and curious protagonist give exploration an optimistic tone, with new routes and discoveries drawing players beyond the next town.

cards.heading: Choosing an optimistic adventure
cards.text: Kodama and the team wanted a brighter adventure than the darker RPGs they saw around them. Vyse's enthusiasm for travel carries that choice into the story, while colour and music reinforce it across the floating islands. War and loss still enter the journey, but curiosity remains a reason to keep sailing. The air pirate setting makes crossing the horizon a central ambition for both character and player.

cards.heading: Discoveries beyond the direct route
cards.text: Discoveries reward attention while sailing: unusual places, creatures and phenomena can be identified and their information sold. A wreck or formation on the horizon can therefore provide a reason to leave the direct route. Finding these details gradually expands the player's knowledge of the sky ocean, turning observation during travel into a useful activity of its own.

cards.heading: Planning the next shipboard turns
cards.text: Ship battles use a different rhythm from party combat. Players plan the crew's turns, deciding when to attack, defend, recover Spirit or fire the main cannon. Coloured indicators warn of dangerous or favourable moments ahead. Ships have statistics and equipment, so preparing a vessel and reading the next turns matter alongside the strength of the people aboard.

cards.heading: A captain builds a crew
cards.text: New ships and recruited crew members expand Vyse's responsibilities as the adventure progresses. Equipment changes affect the vessel, while crew members contribute abilities in combat or support other activities. Meeting people can consequently improve the means of travelling through the world. Building a crew and a base develops the fantasy of becoming a captain alongside the party's individual progress.

cards.heading: A Dreamcast production across two discs
cards.text: Dreamcast allowed the team to develop more detailed models, facial animation and directed scenes for its broad, bright world. The production also planned for an international audience, with localisation and extensive text spread across two GD-ROMs. These demands brought character performance, exploration and cinematic presentation together within an adventure built on the familiar structure of a party RPG.

main.title: Spyro: Year of the Dragon
main.summary: Spyro: Year of the Dragon is a 2000 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation.

cards.heading: Spyro: Year of the Dragon
cards.text: Spyro: Year of the Dragon is a 2000 platform game developed by Insomniac Games and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation. The third installment in the Spyro series, Year of the Dragon follows the adventures of the titular purple dragon. After an evil sorceress steals magical dragon eggs from the land of the dragons, Spyro travels to the "Forgotten Realms" to retrieve them. Players travel across different worlds gathering gems and eggs, defeating enemies, and playing minigames. Year of the Dragon introduced new characters and minigames to the series, as well as offering improved graphics and music.

cards.heading: Insomniac's final PlayStation Spyro
cards.text: Year of the Dragon received critical acclaim, with reviewers noting how the game successfully built upon the formula of its predecessors. The game sold more than 3 million copies worldwide. Year of the Dragon was the last Spyro title released for the original PlayStation, and the last developed by Insomniac Games due to Universal Interactive Studios and Sony's souring relationship. Year of the Dragon was followed by the multiplatform title Spyro: Enter the Dragonfly (2002), and was later remade as part of the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.
